generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, psychology spreads assessment across a module for a reason: some tasks are there to help you improve before the stakes rise, and some set your mark. A formative lab write-up your tutor comments on, a practice statistics quiz, a draft of your research report: these let you act on feedback while it still changes the outcome. Knowing which is which tells you where to take risks and where to consolidate, which is why the distinction is worth getting straight early.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students hand in the same formative draft of a lab report, which the tutor comments on but does not mark.

Tom sees that it does not count and barely reads the comments, saving his effort for the graded version. When the summative report comes back, the same problems the tutor had already flagged, a weak analysis section and an over-claimed conclusion, cost him marks.

Amara treats the formative draft as the cheap chance it is. She works through the tutor's comments, strengthens the analysis and tempers the conclusion, and carries those changes into the summative report. Her graded report is stronger precisely because she used the formative task for what it was for.

Both had the same draft and the same comments. Only Amara used the formative stage to improve the summative one, which is the whole point of splitting them.
generatedProse.summary: Formative assessment is there to help you improve and does not count toward your grade; summative assessment is the task that sets it. In your psychology modules the two work together: a practice quiz or a commented draft of a lab report is where you find out what is not yet working and put it right. By the time the final report or presentation counts, you are already performing at your best. This is what strategic learning means: recognising why each task has been set and what it is preparing you to do, because every formative and summative task is a step towards the same thing, being able to demonstrate your module’s learning outcomes. Once you can see that link, you can tell what any task is really asking of you and spend your effort where it pays.

check.body: Sort each of these psychology assessments by whether it is formative or summative.

items.text: A practice statistics quiz during term that does not count toward your grade
A draft lab report your tutor comments on but does not mark
An assessed presentation at the end of the module
The final research report that sets your module grade

feedback.correct: That's right. Formative assessment is there to help you improve and does not count toward your grade; summative assessment is the task that sets it.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. For each one, ask: does this count toward my final grade, or is it there to help me improve first?
feedback.incorrectFinal: The practice quiz and the commented draft are formative: they help you improve and do not count. The presentation and the final report are summative: they set your grade. The test is simple, does it count toward the mark, or help you reach it?
feedback.partlyCorrectNotFinal: Some of those are right, but not all. Check each one against the question: does it count, or help you improve first?
feedback.partlyCorrectFinal: Formative tasks (the practice quiz, the commented draft) help you improve and do not count; summative tasks (the presentation, the final report) set your grade.
